intuition.text: A take-off marker asks Finch to arrive in a particular moving state. Reaching the painted ring while standing still is no help when the canal crossing needs forward speed. The run-up prepares that speed; the marker grants the vertical jump only when position and velocity agree with its requirement.
intuition.situation: A courier follows a straight quay towards a designer-authored crossing. The marker makes the transition from ground locomotion to airborne motion inspectable and gives an explicit reason to refuse a poorly prepared jump.

example.name: Finch crossing the canal
example.description: Finch begins at {startX} m with horizontal velocity {initialVelocity} m/s and approaches the take-off ring at {markerX} m. The ring requires {requiredVelocity} m/s within {velocityTolerance} m/s and position within {positionTolerance} m. Run-up acceleration is limited to {maxAcceleration} m/s², speed to {maxSpeed} m/s and response time to {responseTime} s. An accepted launch adds vertical velocity {verticalVelocity} m/s under gravity {gravity} m/s². The equal-height receiving pad is centred at {padCentre} m, with half-width {padHalfWidth} m. The current phase is {phase}, horizontal speed {vx} m/s and height {height} m.

steps.title: Author a take-off state
steps.text: Place the ring at {markerX} m and require forward velocity {requiredVelocity} m/s. For this canal, the vertical impulse and equal platform heights imply flight duration {flightDuration} s. Place the receiving pad where that required horizontal velocity carries Finch during the flight. The marker protocol and this trajectory are study-local.

steps.title: Prepare the moving arrival
steps.text: During the straight run-up, call the scene engine’s matchVelocity with the marker’s required velocity. It requests the velocity gap divided by {responseTime} s and caps acceleration. Advance the new horizontal velocity over {timeStep} s. This is a velocity target, so the run-up keeps moving through the ring rather than slowing towards a stop.

steps.title: Check both conditions at the marker
steps.text: At the first sampled encounter with the marker window, check position error and horizontal velocity error together. Only a valid state receives the vertical launch impulse; preserve the actual horizontal velocity instead of replacing it with the requested one. A failed encounter ends this one-pass example as rejected, with no claim to simulate emergency braking.

steps.title: Follow the accepted flight
steps.text: After take-off, horizontal velocity remains constant and height follows the constant-gravity equation. Sample until the equal-height ground contact, then compare the contact position with the receiving pad. The airborne calculation uses elapsed flight time {airTime} s; the current height is {height} m and vertical velocity {vy} m/s. The study stops before landing collision response.

pseudocode.ordinary:
marker = (markerX, requiredVelocity)
flightDuration = 2 * verticalVelocity / gravity
padCentre = markerX + requiredVelocity * flightDuration
state = (startX, initialVelocity, runUp)

while x < markerX - positionTolerance and steps remain:
  acceleration = engine.matchVelocity(body, requiredVelocity, responseTime)
  velocity = clamp(velocity + acceleration * dt, -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)
  x = x + velocity * dt
if the step horizon ends before the marker: report unfinished

positionOK = abs(x - markerX) <= positionTolerance
velocityOK = abs(velocity - requiredVelocity) <= velocityTolerance
if not (positionOK and velocityOK): reject this encounter
takeoffX = x
takeoffVelocity = velocity
apply verticalVelocity as the jump impulse

for each airborne sample t through flightDuration:
  x = takeoffX + takeoffVelocity * t
  height = verticalVelocity * t - gravity * t * t / 2
  vy = verticalVelocity - gravity * t
at ground contact:
  landingError = abs(x - padCentre)
  report whether landingError <= padHalfWidth
  end before collision response

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s Finch is in phase {phase}, x {x} m and height {height} m, with horizontal velocity {vx} m/s and vertical velocity {vy} m/s; the ring at {markerX} m requires {requiredVelocity} m/s, current position error is {positionError} m and velocity error {velocityError} m/s, while the planned arc ends at the receiving pad centred at {padCentre} m.

implementations.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game-AI library. Its Jump behaviour connects an authored take-off and landing descriptor to a velocity-matching run-up and a take-off callback.
implementations.explanation: Jump derives an airborne time and planar velocity from its descriptor and gravity, checks the speed limit, and delegates run-up acceleration to MatchVelocity. calculateRealSteering calls takeoff only after both position and velocity tolerances pass. The callback applies the launch action; the steering calculation does not itself animate the flight.

references.title: AI for Games, third edition · Chapter 3 Movement · §3.6.1 Jump Points
references.supports: The book covers this topic at Chapter 3, §3.6.1, the location recorded by the catalog. DOI metadata confirms the book’s identity and edition; no chapter text was read or used for the local marker policy.

references.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · Jump.java
references.supports: A concrete jump behaviour checks position and velocity tolerances before invoking takeoff, and delegates its approach acceleration to velocity matching.

references.title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 · §4.3 Projectile Motion
references.supports: Under constant downward gravity and negligible air resistance, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical position is initial vertical velocity times time minus half gravity times time squared; equal-height flight duration follows from that equation.

limits: A marker does not supply the runway needed to reach its required velocity. Starting at {lateStartX} m can reach the ring with too much velocity error; the comparison rejects launch rather than silently supplying the missing horizontal speed.

The runway is straight and aligned with the required velocity. This one-dimensional run-up uses engine velocity matching, not a general controller that synchronises an arbitrary position and velocity in space.

The gate is tested at sampled positions. A coarse step can skip a narrow position window even with the correct speed; the one-pass policy then rejects the encounter. A production controller could plan an event crossing or retry, but neither occurs here.
An accepted state is within tolerances, rather than necessarily exact. Its actual launch position and velocity determine contact, so an especially narrow receiving pad can still be missed.

The flight assumes equal platform heights, constant gravity and no air resistance or mid-air control. The terminal sample ends at contact before collision response; this local marker protocol is not a scene-engine jumping feature.

nearby.why: Landing pads becomes useful when the receiving region and its tolerances should determine the launch requirement, rather than merely checking this authored crossing.
Velocity matching explains the engine acceleration that prepares the run-up; use it alone when matching motion is enough and no jump transition is needed.
Take-off velocity matching focuses on reaching the required moving state, especially when the runway, acceleration limit or timing makes that state difficult to obtain.
Arrive is appropriate when Finch should stop at a destination. A launch marker instead requires forward motion at the encounter.
